title: A Big Vote in Maine: Why One Senator's Court Choice Still Matters
summary: Have you ever made a choice that years later still follows you around? That's happening right now in Maine, a state in the northeastern U.S. Senator Susan Collins is running for her sixth term, and her 2018 vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court is a big issue. Why? Because that court later overturned Roe v. Wade, the 1973 ruling that had protected abortion rights across the country. After that 2022 decision, abortion became banned in much of the United States. Collins is a Republican, but she supports abortion rights. Still, some voters feel betrayed. Erin Evans, 56, from Portland, voted for Collins in the past. Now she says, "I was a really uninformed voter." This time she's backing Democrat Troy Jackson, a former state lawmaker and logger. Democrats hope voters like Evans will help them win a Senate seat. But Collins is a tough opponent. She has won elections for 30 years, even when Maine voters chose Democratic presidents. Money is pouring in: one group spent nearly $10 million on ads about Collins and judges, and another spent $32 million. The election is November 3.
why_it_matters: It shows that the people we vote for make choices that can change the rules for everyone for many years, so paying attention to elections really matters.

background_read: Maine (a state in the northeastern United States, known for its coast and forests) is small, but its Senate races get attention from the whole country.
The Supreme Court (the highest court in the United States) makes decisions that apply to everyone, and its judges serve for life, so they stay in their jobs for many years.
Roe v. Wade was a 1973 Supreme Court ruling that protected abortion rights across the country until it was overturned in 2022.
Article_Structure: WHO: Senator Susan Collins, voters like Erin Evans, Democrat Troy Jackson, and the Supreme Court justice Brett Kavanaugh.
WHAT: Collins is running for a sixth term while voters argue about her 2018 vote to confirm Kavanaugh, which was followed by the end of nationwide abortion rights.
WHERE: In Maine, a state in the northeastern United States.
WHY: The seat could change which party has power in the Senate, and many voters are thinking about how one court vote changed abortion laws across the country.

perspectives.description: Her backers say she has served Maine for 30 years and has won even when voters picked Democratic presidents, so one vote should not erase her whole record.
Voters like Erin Evans feel betrayed, because the court that Collins helped confirm later overturned Roe v. Wade and abortion became banned in much of the country.
Analysts point out that Maine voters often split their votes between parties, and that huge amounts of money on ads are now part of almost every big Senate race.
